speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry tracks the rates of food allergies in children; (b) if so, what is the current percentage of children who are estimated to have food allergies; (c) what are the trends observed over the last 10 years; and (d) whether the Ministry is undertaking any studies to determine what is causing it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health how is the Ministry working with other agencies such as schools and those in the food preparation industry to increase public awareness of the potentially lethal nature of severe food allergy reactions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is generally lower than the prevalence reported in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are also a number of inter-agency efforts in place to increase awareness on how to better prevent and manage food allergies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: NUH has also been educating and supporting patients and caregivers on food allergies, in partnership with polyclinics, patient support groups and non-profit organisations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The thrust of my question is to understand whether, for example – I understand that in the last five years, there has been found to be a worldwide increase in prevalence of food allergies, especially in children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I am just wondering whether we have similar data in Singapore, because I note that a Straits Times article that was published recently, also stated that, for example, in 2014, I think there were 300 cases seen by one of the hospitals, and by 2020, it has gone up to 10,000.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, again, trying to understand how much of that is due to, I guess, actual increase or how much of it is just increased public awareness?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will be helpful for us to know.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second question really relates to the food handling industry and people who handle food in general.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has just been my experience that sometimes, even when we make it known in advance that we do have food allergies among one of the diners, there are times when, on occasion, we have actually been served with the allergen in question, when we specifically said that one of us is severely allergic to it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That is obviously far from ideal when it was a very near miss on one occasion when the food was literally almost put into the mouth.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I hope that more awareness can be raised around this issue.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On other occasions, we have also been met with incomprehension from either from food waitresses or food handlers who literally do not understand what we are trying to tell them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I think that more work needs to be done from this perspective.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Other countries have taken the route of, such as food labelling where common allergens are displayed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I think you do actually find it in some restaurants and some chains – they do have common allergens clearly labelled on menus.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I think that is something that we could also look at.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And again, the Senior Minister of State earlier mentioned MOE and ECDA.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think if I am not wrong, ECDA has training for preschool teachers, where they train the use of the EpiPen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That is great because that by extension, that means that early childhood educators are aware of how to spot food allergies and how to handle that.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I think, again, from my understanding of the situation, certain schools are probably a bit more advanced in terms of the public education and the initiatives that they have taken, especially in the primary school level, to educate, both students and teachers, and also the food handlers within the canteens, about their importance; because even though the numbers might be small, each one incident can be potentially life threatening.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I hope that the Senior Minister of State can also let us know about when they are expecting to roll out more of these national initiatives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think we would all agree, and I certainly do, that we should continue to educate and raise awareness on matters such as this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, the various agencies and training providers for the workers, whether they are food handlers or early childhood educators, people in a position of responsibility around food and vulnerable people – this is an issue and it is something that we will have to continue to do and to continue to improve on, and learn from the lessons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, for the second part of her question, there is no disagreement.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the absolute numbers may not necessarily be the correct reflection.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: More importantly, our dietary patterns and the practices around how we raise our children have changed quite significantly over the last two generations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In two of these factors, one, for example, is the issue of when to introduce allergens into the diet.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It was not always so that that was the guidance and so the people who are my age and, perhaps, a little bit younger, were brought up under a slightly different approach.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that will lead to a change in our prevalence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Similarly, how we deal with hygiene in the environment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have now come to the realisation that there is some benefit for young children to be exposed to, for example, outdoor environments and unstructured play, and places which, perhaps, my generation were used to, and which the generation in between would have seen as inappropriately dirty and not adequately sanitised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We now know that there is some benefit for children to play in the outdoors, with some degree of dirt – this is known as the hygiene hypothesis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Well, we do need to pay attention to this issue of allergies in general and we do not want our population to be inappropriately exposed to some of the risks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are taking appropriate steps and the most important thing that we can do is provide the right kind of guidance.
